newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian ringgit rises on fresh fund demand.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian ringgit rises on fresh fund demand.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit has emerged from a fortnight-long correction to resume its rise against the U.S. dollar on fresh demand from overseas funds and supportive official comments, dealers said on Wednesday.

Strong economic fundamentals, high local interest rates and problems in other Asian economies had returned the ringgit to its spot as the region's favourite currency among overseas investors, they said.
Since Monday, the ringgit has gained nearly 100 points and is expected to rise further this week.
At 0700 GMT, the ringgit was at 2.4890/00 a dollar.
"(It) is on course to break below 2.48 (per dollar) in the next one week," said Desmond Supple, regional economist with research firm I.D.E.A. in Singapore.
The ringgit hit a 17-month high of 2.4680 a dollar on January 13 on sustained buying by overseas funds.
Expectations of a weaker U.S. dollar had fuelled the ringgit's rise this week, he said.
The expectations came after finance ministers from the Group of Seven (G7) developed nations last week called for a stop to the dollar's runaway rise against other major currencies.

Many U.S. funds, which had reduced their ringgit holdings before the Chinese Lunar New Year and Moslem Eid al-Fitr holidays from February 7 to 11 in Malaysia, were also selling the Singapore dollar in favour of the ringgit.
The dealers and analysts said more important for the ringgit, however, was support from Malaysia's Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
He said on Tuesday that Malaysia was not worried about the ringgit's rise against the U.S. dollar.

"The economy is strong and the ringgit seems to be strengthening against the U.S. dollar. I don't think it is an issue that should be highlighted or be overly concerned about," the daily New Straits Times quoted him as saying.
"The ringgit is not reacting today despite the strong dollar/majors because of Anwar's comments," said an European bank dealer in Singapore.
"It (the comment) reaffirms the government's preference for a strong ringgit. It gives a hint to the market that there is upside potential for the ringgit," Supple said.
He said investors were attracted to the ringgit because "apart from positive yield differential, there is the added potential of capital gains".
The benchmark three-month interbank rate in Kuala Lumpur is more than four percentage points higher than in Singapore.
The head of dealing at a Malaysian bank said the ringgit could continue gaining in the next few weeks if Malaysia's interest rates remained high.
He said economic woes in neighbouring Thailand and intervention band restrictions in Indonesia were also boosting the ringgit.

Malaysia recorded a sharply lower trade deficit of 1.5 billion ringgit ($600 million) in the first 11 months of 1996 against around 10 billion ringgit ($4 billion) in the corresponding period of 1995.

Malaysia's 1996 gross domestic product growth is expected to fall to 8.2 percent, following 9.5 percent growth in 1995. The country has reported nine straight years of growth over eight percent, which is expected to be maintained until the year 2000.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 8911) ($1 = 2.49 ringgit)
